Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands on your machine or directly interact with external services such as GitHub.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally to accomplish everything you described.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Generate Files

### 2.1 Inspect the Project

Open the repo in your favourite editor (VS Code, Vim, etc.) and look for:

| File | What to look for |
|------|------------------|
| `package.json` | Dependencies, start script (`scripts.start`) |
| `app.js` / `index.js` | Entry point, port listening logic |
| `.env.example` | Environment variables |
| `README.md` | Any deployment hints |

> **Common patterns**  
> *If the start script is `"start": "node app.js"`* → entrypoint is `node app.js`.  
> *If the app listens on `process.env.PORT || 3000`* → expose port `3000`.

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the repo root (or update it if it already exists):

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> *Node 18‑alpine* is lightweight and includes the LTS version of Node.  
> `npm ci` installs exactly what’s in `package-lock.json`, ensuring reproducible builds.  
> The `EXPOSE` line matches the typical port used in Node examples (`3000`).  
> Adjust the port if your app uses a different one.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you may need to create the `k8s` folder):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: nodejs-welcome-secrets   # optional: load secrets
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to replace**  
> * `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` – e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`.  
> * `nodejs-welcome-secrets` – create a Kubernetes Secret if you need environment variables that shouldn’t be in plain text.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
        images: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        namespace: default
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token.  
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig for the cluster you’re deploying to.  

> **Why this workflow?**  
> *Runs on pushes to `main`.*  
> *Builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub.*  
> *Deploys the new image to Kubernetes using the manifest you created.*

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you added a `k8s` folder, make sure it’s tracked:  
> ```bash
> git add k8s
> ```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger and build/push the Docker image.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

1. A Dockerfile that builds a lightweight image for your Node.js app.  
2. Kubernetes deployment/service YAML ready for a LoadBalancer.  
3. A GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image on every push to `main` and deploys it.

Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile, YAML, or workflow to match your exact requirements (e.g., different base image, more environment variables, or a different Kubernetes namespace).
